1.topic: The main parts of a computer
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. name the main parts of a computer system;
2. say what the CPU does;
3. give examples of input, output and storage devices;
4. sort devices into input, output and storage.

## Materials

A desktop computer (or pictures of one), a keyboard, mouse, flash drive, printer and a set of picture cards of devices.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: "When you send a text message on a phone, what do you do first, and what do you see after?" Lead pupils to see that something goes in, something is done to it, and something comes out.

## Development

1. Show the system unit, monitor, keyboard and mouse. Explain that a computer takes in data, processes it and gives out information.
2. Input devices send data in: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone.
3. The CPU is the brain of the computer. It carries out instructions and does the calculations.
4. Output devices show results: monitor, printer, speaker.
5. Storage devices keep files so they are not lost when the computer is switched off: hard disk, flash drive, memory card.
6. Memory (RAM) holds what the computer is working on at the moment and is cleared when power goes off.

## Class activity

Groups receive picture cards and sort them into three columns: input, output, storage. Each group explains one card they found hard.

## Evaluation

1. What does the CPU do?
2. Give two input devices and two output devices.

## Assignment

Complete the worksheet on the app and list five devices found in your home and say which group each belongs to.

reading.title: Meet the parts of a computer
reading.content:
# The main parts of a computer

A computer is a machine that takes in **data**, works on it, and gives out **information**. To do this it uses four groups of parts.

## Input devices

Input devices send data **into** the computer. The **keyboard** sends the letters you type. The **mouse** sends the movement of your hand so you can point and click. A **scanner** copies a page into the computer, and a **microphone** sends sound.

## The CPU

CPU stands for **Central Processing Unit**. It is the brain of the computer. It follows instructions and does all the calculations. When you add two numbers in a calculator program, the CPU does the adding. A faster CPU means the computer finishes work more quickly.

## Output devices

Output devices show you the result. The **monitor** shows pictures and words on a screen. The **printer** puts the words on paper. The **speaker** gives out sound.

## Storage devices

Storage devices keep your work so you can open it later, even after the computer is switched off. Examples are the **hard disk** inside the computer, the **flash drive** you plug in, and the **memory card** in a phone.

## Memory is not the same as storage

The computer's **memory (RAM)** holds the work you are doing right now. When the power goes off, for example during a NEPA light-out, whatever was not saved is lost. That is why you must **save** your work to a storage device.

## Example

A pupil in Abeokuta types a short story on the keyboard (input). The CPU processes it. The story appears on the monitor (output). She saves it on a flash drive (storage). Later she prints it on the printer (output).

2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. say the difference between hardware and software;
2. name the two kinds of software, system and application;
3. give examples of each kind;
4. say why a computer cannot work with hardware alone.

## Materials

A computer with the operating system on screen, a word processor and a browser open, and cards with the names of programs and devices.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Hold up a keyboard and then a game on a phone screen. Ask: "Which one can I touch and which one can I only see and use?"

## Development

1. Hardware is every part of the computer that you can touch: monitor, keyboard, CPU, mouse.
2. Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. You cannot touch it.
3. System software runs the computer itself. The operating system (Windows, Android, macOS) is the main example. Utility programs such as antivirus also belong here.
4. Application software helps you do a task: a word processor to write, a browser to search the internet, a calculator, a game.
5. Show on the computer: the operating system starts first, and then applications run on top of it.

## Class activity

Pupils sort cards into hardware, system software and application software. Each group defends one card.

## Evaluation

1. Give two examples of hardware and two of software.
2. What does an operating system do?

## Assignment

Complete the worksheet on the app. At home, list the software on a phone and say which is system and which is application.

reading.title: Hardware, software and the two kinds of software
reading.content:
# Hardware and software

## Hardware

**Hardware** is every part of a computer that you can see and touch. The monitor, keyboard, mouse, printer, flash drive and the CPU are all hardware. If it can fall on your foot, it is hardware.

## Software

**Software** is the set of instructions, called programs, that tells the hardware what to do. You cannot touch software. You see what it does on the screen. A computer with no software is like a danfo with a driver who has no road map: the parts are there, but nothing useful happens.

## Two kinds of software

### System software

System software looks after the computer itself. The most important is the **operating system (OS)**. It starts when you switch on, controls the hardware, and lets other programs run. Windows, macOS, Linux and Android are operating systems. **Utility programs**, such as antivirus and disk cleaners, also belong to system software.

### Application software

Application software helps you do a job you want to do:

- a **word processor** for writing letters and notes;
- a **spreadsheet** for figures and tables;
- a **web browser** for the internet;
- a **calculator**, a **music player**, a **game**.

## Working together

When you press the power button, the operating system loads first. Then you open an application, such as a word processor. The application asks the operating system to use the keyboard, screen and storage.

## Worked example

A trader in Ibadan uses a phone to record her sales.
- The phone itself is **hardware**.
- Android, which runs the phone, is **system software**.
- The notes app where she writes her sales is **application software**.

## Remember

Hardware is what you touch. Software is what you run. System software runs the computer. Application software runs your task.

reading.title: Where does the computer keep its files?
reading.content:
# Storage devices and their capacity

## Why we need storage

When the power goes off, a computer forgets what it was working on unless you have **saved** it. A **storage device** keeps your files safely, even when the computer is switched off.

## Common storage devices

**Hard disk drive (HDD).** This is inside most desktop computers. It has a metal disk that spins. It can hold a lot of data and is cheap, but it can be damaged if it is dropped, because of the moving parts.

**Solid state drive (SSD).** This has no moving parts. It starts programs much faster, uses less power, and is not easily damaged by shaking. It usually costs more for the same size.

**Flash drive.** A small stick that plugs into the USB port. It is very good for carrying files from school to home.

**Memory card.** A tiny card used in phones, cameras and tablets to add more space.

## How much can they hold?

We measure storage in **bytes**. One byte holds one letter or number.

| Unit | Size (about) |
|---|---|
| 1 KB (kilobyte) | 1000 bytes |
| 1 MB (megabyte) | 1000 KB |
| 1 GB (gigabyte) | 1000 MB |
| 1 TB (terabyte) | 1000 GB |

A short text file may be a few KB. A photo may be 2 to 5 MB. A film may be 1 or 2 GB. A school's records for many years may need a few TB.

## Worked example

A flash drive holds 8 GB. Each photo is 4 MB. How many photos can fit?

8 GB is about 8000 MB. Then 8000 ÷ 4 = **2000 photos**.

## Choosing a device

- To carry a project from school to home: a **flash drive**.
- For a phone that is out of space: a **memory card**.
- For a school server that must open quickly: an **SSD**.
- For many years of old records at low cost: a **hard disk**.

A tiny card that adds storage to a phone or camera.
The smallest unit we use. It holds one letter or number.
Byte, KB, MB, GB, TB. Each is about 1000 times bigger than the one before.

4.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. sit in the correct posture to type;
2. place their fingers on the home row;
3. group keys into alphanumeric, function and service keys;
4. use common service keys (Shift, Enter, Backspace, Caps Lock, Spacebar).

## Materials

A keyboard chart, computers with a word processor open, and a typing tutor program if available.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask two pupils to type their names, one using one finger and the other using both hands. Ask the class what they notice about speed and comfort.

## Development

1. Posture: sit up straight, feet flat on the floor, elbows near a right angle, wrists level, and the screen at eye level about an arm's length away.
2. Home row: the left fingers rest on A, S, D, F and the right on J, K, L and ;. The thumbs rest on the spacebar. The little bumps on F and J guide the fingers.
3. Alphanumeric keys are the letters and numbers.
4. Function keys F1 to F12 are on the top row; each does a special job in a program, for example F5 refreshes a page.

# Typing posture and the keyboard

Typing well is a skill. If you learn it properly now, you will work faster and your hands and back will not hurt.

## Correct posture

- Sit **upright** with your back against the chair.
- Keep your **feet flat** on the floor.
- Keep your **elbows** bent at about a right angle.
- Keep your **wrists straight**, not bent up or down.
- The **screen** should be at eye level and about an arm's length away.

## The home row

The home row is the middle row of letters. Your fingers rest there when you are not typing.

- Left hand: **A S D F**
- Right hand: **J K L ;**
- Both thumbs: the **spacebar**

There are small bumps on **F** and **J**. You can feel them without looking, so your fingers always know where home is. After pressing a key, return the finger to home.

## Groups of keys

**Alphanumeric keys.** These are the letters A to Z and the numbers 0 to 9, with punctuation.

**Function keys.** F1 to F12 along the top. Each does a special job that depends on the program. For example, F5 refreshes a web page and F1 usually opens Help.

**Service keys.** These help you to edit and control your typing:

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| Enter | Starts a new line or accepts a command |
| Backspace | Deletes the character to the left |
| Delete | Deletes the character to the right |
| Shift | Hold it down to type a capital letter or the top symbol on a key |
| Caps Lock | Keeps all letters in capitals until you press it again |
| Spacebar | Puts a space between words |
| Tab | Jumps across the line |
| Esc | Cancels or escapes |

## Worked example

To type **Lagos is big**: hold **Shift** and press **L**, release, then type *agos*, press the **Spacebar**, type *is*, press the **Spacebar**, and type *big*.

If you type *Lagoss* by mistake, press **Backspace** once to remove the extra *s*.

reading.content:
# Computer networks: LAN, MAN and WAN

## What is a network?

A **computer network** is two or more computers joined together so that they can share things. They can share files, a printer, and an internet connection.

Without a network, a school with 30 computers would need 30 printers. With a network, one printer serves everyone.

## Types of network

### LAN: Local Area Network

A LAN covers a **small area**: one room, a building, a school or a house. The computers in the school's ICT lab form a LAN. One organisation owns it. Because the distances are short, a LAN is usually **fast**.

### MAN: Metropolitan Area Network

A MAN covers a **town or city**. It joins several LANs. For example, the branches of a bank in Kano may be joined in one MAN so that a customer can be served at any branch.

### WAN: Wide Area Network

A WAN covers a **very large area**: a country or the whole world. The **internet** is the largest WAN in the world. Because data travels very far, a WAN is usually **slower** and costs more to run than a LAN.

## How a network works

- **Cable or Wi-Fi** carries the data between devices.
- A **switch** joins the computers inside a LAN.
- A **router** joins one network to another, and connects the LAN to the internet.

Data is sent in small pieces called **packets**. The router sends each packet towards the computer it is meant for, and the other computer puts the pieces back together.

## Speed

Network speed is measured in **megabits per second (Mbps)**. A higher number means more data every second.

## Worked example

A secondary school in Ado-Ekiti joins 25 computers in its lab with cables and a switch. This is a **LAN**. The head teacher connects the lab to the internet through a router. The internet is a **WAN**.

## Why networks are useful

- Share **files** and **printers**.
- Share one **internet** connection.
- **Talk** to each other by email or chat.

reading.content:
# Word processing: create, format, edit and save

A **word processor** is application software for writing and changing documents. Microsoft Word, Google Docs and WPS Writer are examples. A document can be a letter, a notice, a story or a homework.

## Starting a document

Open the program and choose **Blank document**. You will see a white page, a blinking line called the **cursor**, and a **ribbon** of buttons on top. Click on the page and start to type.

## Formatting text

**Formatting** changes how text looks. First **select** the text by dragging over it with the mouse. Then use the buttons.

- **Font and size**: the style and size of the letters.
- **Bold (Ctrl+B)**: makes the text thick.
- **Italic (Ctrl+I)**: slants the text.
- **Underline (Ctrl+U)**: puts a line under the text.
- **Alignment**: left, centre, right or justify (straight on both edges).

A heading is often **bold**, bigger and **centred**.

## Editing text

**Editing** means changing what you have typed.

| Action | Shortcut | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Copy | Ctrl+C | Makes a copy of the selected text |
| Cut | Ctrl+X | Removes the text and keeps it to paste |
| Paste | Ctrl+V | Puts the copied or cut text at the cursor |
| Undo | Ctrl+Z | Takes back the last action |

## Saving

If you do not save, your work can be lost when NEPA takes the light. Press **Ctrl+S**, choose a folder, type a **file name**, and click **Save**. Give names that tell you what the file is, such as *JSS1_Cultural_Day_Notice*, not *Document1*.

**Save As** saves a copy under a new name or in another place, and leaves the first file as it was.

## Worked example

To write a notice:
1. Type *CULTURAL DAY*. Select it, press **Ctrl+B**, choose size 20, and click **Centre**.
2. Press **Enter** and type the details in size 12, left aligned.
3. If you copy the wrong line, press **Ctrl+Z**.
4. Press **Ctrl+S** and save as *JSS1_Cultural_Day_Notice*.

# Spreadsheets: data, formulas and charts

A **spreadsheet** is a program for working with numbers, lists and tables. Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets and WPS Spreadsheets are examples. Traders, banks and teachers use them to add, compare and keep records.

## Parts of a spreadsheet

- **Column**: goes down the page and is named with a letter (A, B, C ...).
- **Row**: goes across the page and is named with a number (1, 2, 3 ...).
- **Cell**: the box where a column and a row meet.
- **Cell address**: the column letter and row number, such as **B3**.
- **Range**: a block of cells, written like **B2:B6**, which means from B2 to B6.

## Entering data

Click a cell and type. Press **Enter** to finish. To change what is in a cell, click it and use the formula bar, or double-click it.

## Formulas

A **formula** always begins with an **equals sign (=)**. It tells the spreadsheet to calculate.

| Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|
| =B2+B3 | Add the numbers in B2 and B3 |
| =B2*C2 | Multiply the numbers in B2 and C2 |
| =SUM(B2:B6) | Add all the numbers from B2 to B6 |

When you change a number the formula uses, the answer changes **automatically**.

## Worked example

A trader in Bodija market records the number of baskets of tomatoes sold in a week.

| | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Day | Baskets |
| 2 | Monday | 12 |
| 3 | Tuesday | 8 |
| 4 | Wednesday | 15 |
| 5 | Thursday | 10 |
| 6 | Friday | 20 |

In cell B7 type **=SUM(B2:B6)**. The answer is 12 + 8 + 15 + 10 + 20 = **65 baskets**. If Tuesday's figure is corrected to 10, the total changes to 67 by itself.

## Charts

A **chart** shows data as a picture. Select the data, click **Insert**, and choose a chart.
- A **column or bar chart** compares amounts, such as sales on each day.
- A **pie chart** shows parts of a whole.

Always give the chart a **title** and label the axes.

# Formatting cells and saving spreadsheets

A spreadsheet with correct numbers can still be hard to read. **Formatting** makes it clear. **Saving** keeps your work so that you can use it again.

## Selecting cells

- Drag with the mouse to select a **range**.
- Click a **column letter** to select the whole column.
- Click a **row number** to select the whole row.

Whatever you do next is applied to the selected cells.

## Common formats

**For the heading row:** make it **bold**, add a **fill colour** and centre it so that it stands out.

**Column width:** if you see #### in a cell, the column is too narrow. Double-click the line between two column letters to fit the column to the data.

**Borders:** these draw lines around cells so that a printed table looks like a table.

**Number formats:**

| Format | Typed | Shown |
|---|---|---|
| Number, 2 decimal places | 1500 | 1500.00 |
| Currency (₦) | 1500 | ₦1,500.00 |
| Percentage | 0.25 | 25% |
| Date | 14/10/2026 | 14-Oct-26 |

The format changes only the look. The value in the cell stays the same, so formulas still work.

## Saving a spreadsheet

1. Press **Ctrl+S** (or File, then Save).
2. Choose a folder.
3. Type a **file name** that says what it is, such as *JSS1_Canteen_Sales*.
4. Keep the file type as **Excel Workbook (.xlsx)** and click **Save**.

After that, **Ctrl+S** updates the same file. Save often, since the light can go off at any time.

**Save As** makes a copy under another name or place, for example to keep an old version.

## Opening a saved file

Click **File**, then **Open**, find the folder, and double-click the file. Recent files are listed so you can open them quickly.

## Worked example

A canteen sold 4 plates of rice at ₦800 each. In cell B2 type 800. Select B2, choose **Currency**, and it will show **₦800.00**. In C2 the formula =B2*4 shows **₦3,200.00**.

# Presentation slides: create, format and present

A **presentation** is a set of **slides** that you show while you talk. Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides and WPS Presentation are programs for making them. Teachers, business people and pupils use slides to explain ideas.

## Starting

Open the program and choose **Blank Presentation**. The first slide is the **title slide**. Click the boxes to type a title and your name.

## Adding slides

Click **New Slide**. Each slide has a **layout**, which is the arrangement of its boxes.

- **Title Slide**: a big title and a small subtitle.
- **Title and Content**: a heading with bullet points.
- **Two Content**: two columns, useful for comparing.
- **Blank**: an empty slide for a picture.

## Writing on slides

Slides are not pages of a book. Keep text **short**.

- Use **3 to 5 bullet points** on a slide.
- Write **key words**, not full sentences.
- Use **one idea** on each slide.
- Use a font size of **24 or more** so people at the back can read.

## Design

A **theme** gives all the slides the same colours and fonts. Pick one theme for the whole presentation. Choose letters that **contrast** with the background: dark letters on a light background, or the other way round. Avoid yellow on white, because it is very hard to see.

## Showing the slides

- Press **F5** to start the **slide show** from the first slide.
- Use the **arrow keys** or click to move forward and back.
- Press **Esc** to end the show.

## Worked example

A pupil makes slides about Lagos.
- Slide 1 (Title Slide): *Lagos, my city*, with her name.
- Slide 2 (Title and Content): *Transport* with the points *Danfo buses*, *Okada*, *Ferry*.
- Slide 3: *Food* with the points *Jollof rice*, *Akara*, *Suya*.

Each slide has one idea and few words, so it is easy to read.
